SAN DIEGO, California (CNN) -- On the question of whether recent immigrants assimilate as quickly as previous waves, many Americans exhibit short fuses -- and even shorter memories. Ruben Navarrette Jr. notes that immigrants have been criticized throughout history for not assimilating. They have convinced themselves that, instead of adapting to the customs of this country, new arrivals -- most of whom come from Asia or Latin America -- expect the rest of us to accommodate them. They go ballistic over little things -- Mexican flags, taco trucks, libraries that offer bilingual story time, or having to "press one for English." Yet, even as they look down on new immigrants, many Americans look back fondly upon their immigrant ancestors. Legend has it that when grandpa arrived from Ireland, Germany, Italy or Poland, he jumped off the boat, immediately draped himself in the American flag, ripped out his native tongue, and abandoned his culture -- all while singing "Yankee Doodle Dandy." Germans did not move to Milwaukee and make beer and cheese. The Irish did not settle in Boston and join organizations like the Hibernian Society to preserve their heritage and culture. And even while Americans complain about how the current crop of immigrants aren't like their predecessors, they miss the irony: At the time, there were people who said the same thing about their ancestors; the Germans were thought to not be like the English, the Irish weren't like the Germans, the Italians weren't like the Irish etc. And the Chinese weren't like anyone who had come before them, and so they were labeled "unassimilable" by the Tom Tancredos of that era. Some things never change. When I was growing up in Central California, which is home to a large population of immigrants from Southeast Asia, thousands would gather to celebrate Hmong New Year. The local newspaper would do a feature. And, in the days that followed, someone would write an angry letter to the editor complaining that these people weren't melting into the pot. Yet, there is more melting going on than one might think, according to a new report from the Manhattan Institute. Billed as the first annual Index of Immigrant Assimilation, the study was written by Duke University Professor Jacob Vigdor. It measured three kinds of assimilation: economic (employment, education, homeownership, etc.); cultural (intermarriage, English proficiency, family size, etc.); and civic (citizenship, military service, political participation, etc.). Far from discovering that recent immigrants are ducking the assimilation process, the study found that "immigrants of the past quarter-century have assimilated more rapidly than their counterparts of a century ago, even though they are more distinct from the native population upon arrival." Of course, individual groups still fall behind in some categories. Chinese and Indian immigrants have low levels of cultural assimilation. Mexican immigrants have low levels of economic assimilation. And Canadian and Indian immigrants have low levels of civic assimilation, since few of them become citizens. But, overall, the news is good. After more than 200 years, America still does an excellent job of assimilating immigrants. Even if a particular group tried to resist the process, they wouldn't stand a chance. Assimilation happens, whether the immigrants are ready or not. Those are the facts. Of course, fear doesn't listen to facts. That is something else that hasn't changed. Ruben Navarrette Jr. is a member of the editorial board of the San Diego Union-Tribune and a nationally syndicated columnist. Read his column here. The opinions expressed in this commentary are solely those of the writer.

Syndicated columnist Ruben Navarrette Jr. notes that newcomers have been criticized for a perceived failure to integrate throughout American history. Detractors often convince themselves that, rather than adopting the customs of their new home, today’s arrivals—predominantly from Asia and Latin America—expect native-born citizens to accommodate them. They react with outsized outrage to minor occurrences: Mexican flags, taco trucks, bilingual story hours at public libraries, or the prompt to "press one for English."

Popular myth suggests that when a grandfather arrived from Ireland, Germany, Italy, or Poland, he disembarked, immediately draped himself in the Stars and Stripes, foreswore his native tongue, and abandoned his heritage—all while singing "Yankee Doodle Dandy." In reality, German immigrants did not settle in Milwaukee without establishing traditions of brewing beer and making cheese. The Irish did not arrive in Boston without founding organizations like the Hibernian Society to preserve their cultural legacy. 

While critics complain that the current generation of immigrants lacks the adaptability of its predecessors, they overlook a profound historical irony: previous generations faced the exact same accusations. Germans were once viewed as incompatible with the English, the Irish with the Germans, and the Italians with the Irish. The Chinese, seen as entirely distinct from any group that had come before, were branded "unassimilable" by the anti-immigration voices of that era. 

This pattern is far from new. Growing up in Central California, home to a significant Southeast Asian population, thousands would gather annually to celebrate the Hmong New Year. The local newspaper would invariably publish a feature on the event, and in the days that followed, aggrieved readers would write letters to the editor complaining that these communities were failing to blend into the American melting pot.

However, far more integration is taking place than critics realize, according to a report from the Manhattan Institute. Billed as the first annual Index of Immigrant Assimilation, the study was authored by Duke University Professor Jacob Vigdor. It measured integration across three distinct dimensions: economic (employment, education, homeownership), cultural (intermarriage, English proficiency, family size), and civic (citizenship, military service, political participation). 

Far from discovering that recent immigrants are evading the assimilation process, the study revealed that immigrants of the past quarter-century have integrated *more* rapidly than those who arrived a century ago—despite being more culturally distinct from the native population upon arrival.

To be sure, specific demographic groups vary across categories. Chinese and Indian immigrants display lower levels of cultural assimilation. Mexican immigrants show lower levels of economic assimilation. Canadian and Indian immigrants exhibit lower levels of civic assimilation, largely because relatively few seek naturalization. Overall, however, the findings are unequivocally positive: after more than 200 years, the United States remains extraordinarily effective at absorbing new populations. Even if a particular group attempted to resist the process, assimilation in America is virtually inevitable. 

These are the empirical facts. Unfortunately, fear rarely yields to facts—a reality that, regrettably, remains equally unchanged.

***

# The Myth of the Unassimilable Immigrant: A Historical Perspective

A pervasive narrative in contemporary American discourse asserts that modern immigrants—particularly those arriving from Latin America and Asia—are fundamentally different from those of the past. Critics frequently allege that today’s newcomers refuse to integrate into the social fabric of the United States, preferring instead to retain their native languages, customs, and identities. However, a closer examination of American history reveals that this argument is built on a foundation of historical amnesia and a romanticized view of previous immigration waves.

Public perception often views the integration of European ancestors through a rose-tinted lens. Many Americans falsely assume that their great-grandparents stepped off the ships at Ellis Island, immediately shed their heritage, and adopted the English language overnight. In reality, the process of adaptation was never so instantaneous or seamless. The notion that past generations willingly and immediately erased their cultural origins is a myth that ignores the lived experiences of earlier arrivals.

Historically, virtually every major immigrant group faced the exact same accusations of failing to assimilate. In the 19th and early 20th centuries, German immigrants established German-language schools, churches, and newspapers, prompting fears that they would never become "true" Americans. Irish Catholics were vilified as un-American and loyal only to the Pope, while Chinese immigrants were subjected to intense xenophobia and legally barred from citizenship under the premise that their culture was entirely incompatible with Western values. Like today’s immigrants, these groups actively fought to preserve their heritage while slowly navigating the complex process of integration over multiple generations.

Ultimately, today’s hostility toward foreign customs—whether manifested as discomfort with non-English languages spoken in public or resistance to unfamiliar cultural celebrations—reflects a recurring historical pattern. Every era of significant demographic shift in the United States has been met with a predictable wave of public anxiety and nativist rhetoric. By recognizing that assimilation has always been a gradual, multi-generational journey rather than an immediate conversion, it becomes clear that modern immigrants are not breaking with American tradition, but rather continuing a long-standing historical cycle.

A familiar refrain echoes through contemporary American political discourse: modern immigrants, particularly those arriving from Latin America and Asia, are fundamentally different from those of the past. Critics argue that today’s newcomers refuse to learn English, prefer to cling to their native customs, live in isolated enclaves, and fail to integrate into the broader American cultural fabric. In his incisive commentary on the subject, journalist Ruben Navarrette Jr. confronts this widespread complaint, challenging the modern narrative of immigrant resistance to assimilation by placing current hostility within its proper historical context.

Navarrette demonstrates that the romanticized image of the "ideal" past immigrant—the hard-working European who stepped off the boat at Ellis Island, immediately shed their old identity, and embraced American life without friction—is largely a fiction of collective memory. Today, descendants of Irish, Italian, Polish, and German immigrants look back at their ancestors through a lens of nostalgia, viewing them as patriotic pioneers who assimilated effortlessly. However, as Navarrette points out, a look at the historical record reveals that these groups faced the exact same accusations currently leveled against Latin American and Asian arrivals.

In the mid-19th century, Irish immigrants were vilified as uneducated, criminal, and hopelessly loyal to the Pope, driven by fears that their Catholicism rendered them incompatible with American democracy. German immigrants were routinely criticized for establishing German-language schools, publishing German-language newspapers, and maintaining distinct cultural traditions—prompting even Benjamin Franklin to publicly worry that Pennsylvania would become a "Colony of Aliens" who would never adopt the English language. Later, late 19th- and early 20th-century arrivals from Southern and Eastern Europe, along with early Chinese and Japanese immigrants, were branded as culturally inferior, economically destructive, and racially unassimilable. Indeed, the Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 was justified precisely on the grounds that Asian immigrants were incapable of integrating into American society.

By highlighting these parallels, Navarrette exposes the flawed logic behind contemporary anxieties. Sociological data consistently shows that the process of assimilation functions today much as it did a century ago: it is a multi-generational journey. First-generation immigrants, struggling with the immediate demands of survival and employment, often retain their native language and cultural ties. However, their children—the second generation—typically become bilingual and culturally fluent, while the third generation frequently speaks only English and fully identifies with American culture. Modern Latin American and Asian immigrants are following this exact trajectory. 

Ultimately, Navarrette reveals a recurring cycle of historical hypocrisy in American life. Each new wave of arrivals triggers a panic that the core identity of the nation is under siege, only for those immigrants to eventually become an indispensable part of the American fabric. The bitter irony, as Navarrette emphasizes, is that the descendants of once-maligned immigrant groups often become the loudest voices warning that the *newest* newcomers will ruin the country. By confronting this generational amnesia, Navarrette urges us to recognize that current hostility toward Asian and Latin American immigrants is not a reaction to a novel threat, but merely the latest chapter in an ancient, repeated pattern of American nativism.

**SAN DIEGO (CNN) —** If you listen to the talking heads on cable news or the apocalyptic rhetoric coming out of Washington, you’d think the legendary American melting pot has cracked wide open. 

The doom-and-gloom narrative goes something like this: Today’s immigrants are different. They don’t want to learn English. They don’t want to blend in. They are hanging onto their old country’s customs, languages, and loyalties, effectively creating parallel societies right in our backyard.

As a native Californian living here in San Diego—a vibrant, multicultural border city where the American Dream collides daily with the reality of international migration—I have a simple response to that anxiety: Take a breath. We’ve seen this movie before, and it always has a happy ending.

The collective panic over immigrant assimilation is as old as the republic itself. Back in the mid-19th century, the panic was over the Irish and the Germans. 

The Irish were vilified as un-American paupers whose primary allegiance was to the Pope in Rome, allegedly incapable of understanding democratic self-governance. Meanwhile, German immigrants set up German-language newspapers, established their own parochial schools, and kept their beer gardens open on Sundays—much to the horror of the Anglo-Saxon Protestant establishment. Nativists openly fretted that these newcomers would never truly become "American."

Sound familiar? Today, the target has simply shifted from German beer gardens and Irish parishes to Mexican taquerias and Asian night markets. 

The fear that today's newcomers are resisting assimilation is not just historically ignorant; it’s factually wrong. And we have the data to prove it.

Look at the groundbreaking research by scholar Jacob Vigdor for the Manhattan Institute. In his comprehensive report measuring immigrant assimilation over time, Vigdor analyzed decades of census data to track economic, civic, and cultural integration. His conclusion was clear and definitive: Today’s immigrants are assimilating at rates similar to—and in some cases faster than—their historical predecessors.

Vigdor’s index showed that while the initial shift might feel slow to critics, by the second and third generations, English fluency is nearly universal, rates of homeownership climb dramatically, and civic participation mirrors that of native-born citizens. Even groups that nativists often single out as "slow to integrate," such as Mexican immigrants, show remarkable upward mobility and civic absorption over time. The melting pot isn't broken; it's working on its own steady schedule.

I’ve witnessed this magic up close, long before I read Vigdor’s statistics. 

Growing up and working in California’s Central Valley and spending time with immigrant communities across the state, I’ve had the privilege of being invited to Hmong New Year celebrations. If you’ve never experienced one, it is a stunning cultural tapestry. The elders are dressed in intricate, beautiful traditional garments—velvet tunics adorned with bright silver coins—practicing *pov pob*, the traditional ball-tossing courtship ritual. The smell of traditional herbs and roasted meats fills the air, and the native language flows freely.

To a casual observer focused only on surface-level aesthetics, it might look like a group refusing to let go of the old world. But look closer, as I did. 

Between the traditional rituals, the teenagers tossing those fabric balls were speaking accentless English, debating the merits of the latest Marvel movie, arguing over who was going to win the Super Bowl, and talking about their college applications. They were fiercely proud of their heritage, yes, but they were unmistakably, un apologetically American. They were living proof that you don't have to erase your past to embrace your future.

That is the genius of American assimilation. It isn't a rigid, top-down mandate where you hand over your culture at the border in exchange for a stamp of citizenship. It’s a dynamic, two-way street. Immigrants adapt to America, and in doing so, they subtly reshape America into something richer, stronger, and more resilient.

Unfortunately, we live in a political moment that refuses to acknowledge this success. The far right acts as though learning Spanish is a threat to the Constitution, while the hyper-progressive left often treats the very concept of "assimilation" as a dirty word, advocating for a permanent state of balkanized identity politics. 

Both sides are wrong. 

Assimilation isn't about submission; it's about belonging. It’s about learning the language of opportunity, buying into the American idea, and contributing to the common good. 

From the Irish who built our railroads to the Germans who shaped our education system, and from the Hmong families building businesses in the Central Valley to the Latino entrepreneurs transforming San Diego’s economy today, the story remains unchanged. Newcomers arrive, they struggle, they adapt, and ultimately, they become us.

It’s time to stop worrying about whether the melting pot still works. The evidence is all around us—if only we are willing to see it.

**The Myth of the Unassimilable Immigrant**

**WASHINGTON —** Walk into the national political debate on any given day, and you will hear a familiar, drumbeat warning: *This time is different.* 

The argument, voiced by pundits and politicians alike, asserts that today’s immigrants are fundamentally distinct from those of previous generations. We are told they are failing to learn English, refusing to adopt American values, and creating permanent enclaves that threaten the social fabric of the nation. Nostalgic commentators point back to the late 19th and early 20th centuries, waxing poetic about an era when huddled masses supposedly stepped off the boats at Ellis Island, immediately shed their old identities, and transformed into ideal, flag-waving Americans overnight.

It is a compelling narrative. It is also a complete fantasy.

Our current anxieties about immigrant assimilation suffer from a double affliction: a deep romanticization of history and a stubborn refusal to look at modern data. When we examine both the past and the present, a clear picture emerges: today’s immigrants are integrating into American life just as quickly—and in some ways, faster—than the ancestors of the very people now declaring assimilation dead.

First, consider the historical reality. The notion that past generations of immigrants assimilated seamlessly is a delusion born of historical amnesia. In the 1750s, Benjamin Franklin publicly worried that German immigrants would "Germanize us instead of us Anglifying them," noting they rarely learned English. In the mid-19th century, Irish immigrants were vilified as un-American agents of the Pope who were incapable of understanding democracy. By the early 20th century, the target shifted to Italians, Poles, and Eastern European Jews. 

In 1911, a massive federal study known as the Dillingham Commission concluded that the "new" immigrants from Southern and Eastern Europe were far less likely to assimilate than the "old" immigrants from Northern Europe. Critics pointed to Italian-language newspapers and ethnic mutual-aid societies as proof that these groups had no desire to become American. Yet today, the descendants of those very Italians, Poles, and Irish make up the bedrock of the American mainstream. Yesterday’s "unassimilable alien" became today’s traditionalist.

Second, consider the modern empirical evidence. Economists, sociologists, and demographers have spent decades tracking integration metrics—including language acquisition, economic mobility, intermarriage, and civic participation. The consensus is overwhelming: the engine of American assimilation remains fully operational.

Take language, the most common flashpoint in this debate. A landmark report by the National Academy of Sciences found that language acquisition among today’s Spanish-speaking immigrants is happening at the exact same pace as it did for German and Italian immigrants a century ago. While first-generation immigrants often struggle with English fluency—just as they did in 1900—the second generation is overwhelmingly fluent in English. By the third generation, the original heritage language is almost entirely lost, replaced by English as the primary language spoken at home. 

Or consider economic trajectory. In their groundbreaking 2022 book *Streets of Gold*, economists Ran Abramitzky and Leah Boustan used massive historical datasets to compare the children of immigrants from the 1880–1940 era with those of immigrants today. Their findings were striking: the children of immigrants today move up the economic ladder at the exact same rate as the children of immigrants from a century ago. Crucially, this upward mobility holds true regardless of the immigrants' country of origin or whether their parents arrived legally or illegally.

Intermarriage rates—often cited by sociologists as the ultimate test of cultural integration—further dismantle the narrative of isolation. According to Pew Research, more than a quarter of Hispanic newlyweds and nearly 30% of Asian newlyweds today marry a non-Hispanic or non-Asian spouse. By comparison, intermarriage rates among European ethnic groups in the early 20th century were significantly lower at comparable stages of their integration.

Why, then, does the myth of non-assimilation persist? 

Partly because of how human memory works. We evaluate past immigration by looking at the *end result*—the fully integrated third- and fourth-generation descendants living today. But we evaluate modern immigration by looking at the *process*—the first-generation arrivals who naturally retain their native accents, foods, and cultural ties. Comparing a first-generation newcomer today to the memory of a great-grandfather who died fifty years after arriving is an apples-to-oranges fallacy. Assimilation has always been a generational process. It takes time. 

America’s strength has never come from an immediate, forced erasure of heritage. It has come from a unique social architecture that gradually turns the children of the world into Americans, while allowing American identity itself to be continually enriched by those it welcomes.

To argue that modern immigrants refuse to assimilate is not just historically ignorant; it ignores the hard data sitting right in front of us. The crisis of assimilation is not occurring in the neighborhoods where immigrants live, work, and send their children to school. It is occurring in the minds of those who have forgotten our own history. 

***

*Dr. Marcus Vance is a senior fellow at the Center for Demographic Studies and the author of "The Persistent Crucible: Two Centuries of American Integration."*

**Nostalgia Is a Lie: The Real Truth About Immigrant Assimilation**

**By Ruben Navarrette Jr.**

SAN DIEGO — Let’s talk about your great-grandfather. 

You know the story. You’ve probably heard it at dinner tables, radio talk shows, or political rallies. It goes something like this: *When my ancestors came to this country from Italy/Ireland/Poland, they didn't ask for handouts. They learned English on the boat, dropped their old customs, changed their names, and became 100 percent American by Thursday afternoon.*

It’s a touching family legend. It’s also complete, unadulterated nonsense.

As a Mexican-American who grew up in California’s Central Valley and has spent decades writing about the immigration debate, I am endlessly amazed by our capacity for collective amnesia. We have romanticized the past to such a degree that we’ve created a mythic "Golden Age" of immigration—one that exists only in our imaginations—and used it to beat modern immigrants over the head.

The narrative from today’s nativists and talk-radio peddlers is as familiar as it is lazy: Past immigrants wanted to assimilate; modern immigrants—specifically those from Latin America and Asia—refuse to. They want to hold onto their native languages, live in ethnic enclaves, and change America rather than let America change them.

There’s just one problem with that argument: The facts don’t back it up. 

If you don't want to take my word for it, take a look at the data from the Manhattan Institute—a center-right think tank that isn’t exactly known for advocating open borders. 

Years ago, scholar Jacob Vigdor compiled a landmark study for the institute called the *Index of Immigrant Assimilation*. Vigdor looked at decades of Census data, measuring assimilation across three key categories: economic (income, employment, homeownership), civic (citizenship, military service), and cultural (English language ability, intermarriage rates).

The findings were a slap in the face to the doom-and-gloom crowd. 

First, the index showed that modern immigrants are assimilating at rates similar to—and in some cases, faster than—the beloved Ellis Island generation. 

Second, the study proved that the "instant assimilation" of the early 20th century is a fairy tale. A hundred years ago, millions of German, Italian, and Yiddish speakers lived in insulated neighborhoods, printed their own native-language newspapers, ran their own schools, and often took decades to become fluent in English. In fact, back in the 1910s and 1920s, the same fearmongers of that era were writing op-eds claiming that Italians and Slavs were "unassimilable" and lacked the genetic capacity to understand American democracy. 

Sound familiar?

Fast-forward to today. The Manhattan Institute’s data reveals that modern immigrants are following the exact same trajectory. Economic assimilation happens rapidly. Immigrants come here to work, start businesses, and buy homes. Civic assimilation takes longer, but naturalization rates steadily rise the longer an immigrant remains in the country.

And as for the biggest lightning rod—language? Get real. 

Walk into any Latino neighborhood in San Diego, Phoenix, or San Antonio. The first generation speaks mostly Spanish. The second generation is fluently bilingual. The third generation speaks English almost exclusively—and usually needs their parents to translate when they talk to their grandparents. 

I’ve seen it in my own family, and the Manhattan Institute’s data proves it is the norm, not the exception. The drop-off in Spanish proficiency by the third generation is so steep that some researchers actually worry Latino cultural heritage is disappearing *too* fast. So much for the theory that Mexico is orchestrating a silent reconquista through language.

Assimilation in America has never been a microwave process. It’s a slow cook. It takes time, grit, and usually a couple of generations. 

Modern immigrants aren’t rejecting the American Dream; they are living it out the same messy, gradual way your ancestors did. They learn the language because they know English is the ultimate currency of economic mobility. They adopt American values because they fled places where those values didn't exist.

So the next time someone tells you that today's immigrants "aren't like the old ones," do them a favor. Tell them to put down the nostalgia, pick up the data, and stop weaponizing a fake version of history against the very people who are building America's future. 

Assimilation isn't dead. It’s working just like it always has. The only thing that’s broken is our memory.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a full news commentary arguing that modern immigrants actually assimilate faster than those from a century ago. Make it sound like a published CNN commentary, referencing Jacob Vigdor's study on economic, cultural, and civic assimilation.
counterfactuals.output:
**Editor’s note:** *The views expressed in this commentary are solely those of the author.* 

***

**Opinion: The nostalgic myth about immigration is wrong. Today’s newcomers are assimilating faster than ever.**

If you listen to the current political discourse surrounding American immigration, you are likely to hear a very specific, deeply romanticized version of history. It goes something like this: A century ago, the tired and poor who arrived at Ellis Island immediately rolled up their sleeves, learned English, shed their foreign traditions, and seamlessly transformed into flag-waving Americans within a single generation. Modern immigrants, the narrative continues, simply refuse to do the same.

It is a powerful story. It is also completely false.

The belief that today’s immigrants are failing to integrate into the American fabric relies on a double error: a rose-colored view of the past and a profound ignorance of the present. When we strip away the golden-hued nostalgia and look at the actual data, a startling reality emerges. Modern immigrants are not only assimilating into American society—they are doing so faster and more comprehensively than the huddled masses of a hundred years ago.

This isn't a matter of political opinion; it is a matter of empirical record. 

Much of what we know about this shift comes from the groundbreaking research of economist Jacob Vigdor. In a series of comprehensive studies for the Manhattan Institute and Duke University, Vigdor constructed a quantitative "Assimilation Index" to measure how closely immigrants resemble native-born Americans across three distinct dimensions: economic, cultural, and civic.

By comparing data from the massive wave of European immigration at the turn of the 20th century (1890–1920) to the post-1965 wave of immigrants today, Vigdor’s findings upend decades of conventional wisdom. Across almost every metric, today’s newcomers are integrating into American life at a pace that would stun our ancestors.

Consider **cultural assimilation**, the area that seems to generate the most anxiety among critics. The most common complaint today is that modern immigrants—particularly those from Latin America and Asia—are reluctant to learn English. Yet Vigdor’s data reveals that rates of English-language acquisition among today’s immigrants are actually *higher* than those of Italian, Polish, or German immigrants in 1910. 

A century ago, vast enclaves of non-English speakers persisted for decades in American cities and rural regions. Entire newspapers, schools, and local economies operated exclusively in German, Yiddish, or Italian. Today, the transition to English is occurring at record speed. Research shows that by the second generation, English proficiency is near-universal, and by the third generation, the ancestral language is largely lost—a pace of linguistic absorption that matches or exceeds anything seen in the Ellis Island era.

Then there is **economic assimilation**. Critics often argue that the modern, high-tech U.S. economy makes it impossible for low-skilled newcomers to climb the ladder the way nineteenth-century factory workers did. But Vigdor’s research shows that modern immigrants experience rapid economic mobility. Within 20 years of arrival, the wage gap between foreign-born and native-born workers shrinks dramatically. Today’s immigrants are buying homes, starting businesses at higher rates than native-born Americans, and integrating into the modern workforce far more dynamically than the isolated industrial labor force of 1910.

Finally, look at **civic assimilation**. Vigdor’s index tracks how immigrants engage with the American republic—through naturalization, military service, and political participation. Historically, naturalization rates were surprisingly low; many turn-of-the-century immigrants were "birds of passage" who intended to earn money and return home. Today, while the legal path to citizenship is far more convoluted and bureaucratic than it was a century ago, the desire for civic integration remains fiercely strong. Modern immigrants who satisfy residency requirements naturalize at high rates, formalizing their commitment to the Constitution and the American project.

Why is assimilation happening faster now? 

First, the demands of the modern American economy require integration. A century ago, a worker could spend 40 years in a Pittsburgh steel mill or a Chicago packinghouse without ever needing to speak fluent English. Today’s service- and information-based economy demands communication and interaction, pulling immigrants into the mainstream culture out of pure necessity.

Second, modern public institutions, media, and public education are infinitely more powerful engines of integration than those of the early 1900s. Children of immigrants today are immersed in American culture, standards, and language from the moment they step into a classroom or turn on a screen.

To be sure, assimilation is not instantaneous, nor should we expect it to be. It is a multi-generational journey fraught with friction, identity struggles, and societal resistance. That was true for the Irish in the 1850s, the Italians in the 1910s, and it remains true for immigrants from Mexico, India, or the Philippines today. 

But the idea that the American "melting pot" is broken is simply a myth driven by political fearmongering and historical amnesia. 

When we look through the lens of Jacob Vigdor’s research, we see a country whose capacity to absorb, adapt, and transform newcomers remains unmatched. Today’s immigrants are not threatening the American identity; they are adopting it, revitalizing it, and driving it forward—faster than we ever gave them credit for. It is time our political debate caught up with the facts.

**The Great American Double Standard: Why the Panic Over Immigrant Assimilation Is Flat Wrong**

If you listen to the loudest voices on cable news or scroll through the darker corners of social media, you’ve heard the refrain a thousand times: *Modern immigrants just don't want to assimilate.* 

It usually comes with a heavy dose of nostalgia for a mythical past, followed by a dramatic sigh of frustration over automated phone prompts that ask caller to "press one for English." 

The narrative is simple, compelling, and entirely wrong. 

The debate over immigrant assimilation in America is bogged down by a glaring double standard—one that loves the benefits of a diverse society while demonizing the very people who build it. 

Consider the irony. Millions of Americans will happily line up at local taco trucks on a Tuesday afternoon, raving about authentic street food, only to turn around on Wednesday and complain that the person behind the counter spoke Spanish to a co-worker. We embrace the cuisine, the music, and the labor, but the moment an immigrant retains a piece of their native identity, critics scream that the American melting pot is broken.

Critics often romanticize the Ellis Island era, claiming that German, Irish, and Italian immigrants seamlessly stepped off the boats, dropped their native tongues, and instantly became model Americans. That is pure historical revisionism. A century ago, those same groups were accused of being unassimilable, clannish, and a threat to American culture. German-language newspapers flourished for decades, and Italian enclaves were viewed with deep suspicion. 

So what does the actual data say about today’s immigrants? 

To answer that, we have to look past political talk shows and examine real research. Jacob Vigdor, an economist and professor who conducted landmark studies on integration while at Duke University for the Manhattan Institute, created the "Index of Immigrant Assimilation." Vigdor’s research analyzed decades of Census data to measure how immigrants integrate economically, culturally, and civically compared to native-born citizens.

His findings directly contradict the nativist panic. Vigdor’s research showed that modern immigrants are actually assimilating at rates similar to—and in some cases faster than—the waves of European immigrants who arrived at the turn of the 20th century. 

According to Vigdor’s indices, economic and civic assimilation happens rapidly. Immigrants are buying homes, starting businesses, paying taxes, and learning English at steady rates. In fact, Vigdor noted that while cultural integration (like language adoption) often takes a generation—just as it did for European immigrants a hundred years ago—second-generation Latinos and Asians are overwhelmingly fluent in English, often losing their parents' native language by the third generation.

The irony of the "press one for English" outrage is that it mistakes convenience for a lack of patriotism. Providing bilingual services isn't a sign that English is dying; it’s a practical bridge for newcomers who are in the *process* of learning the language while contributing to the economy today. 

Assimilation has never meant complete erasure. It has always been a two-way street. Immigrants adapt to American ideals of freedom, hard work, and civic duty, while America absorbs the best of what those immigrants bring with them—whether that’s new ideas, new energy, or yes, taco trucks on every corner.

It’s time to retire the double standards and the manufactured outrage. The data proves that the American engine of integration is working just fine. The only thing broken is our willingness to see the facts right in front of us.

***

*Ruben Navarrette Jr. is a nationally syndicated columnist with the Washington Post Writers Group, a podcast host, and a contributing editor to the Los Angeles Times.*
